sections.h2: What are your options for selling a house in Pontiac, Michigan?
sections.html:
A Pontiac owner can list the house, sell it privately, or work with a company that buys houses directly. Pontiac is also the Oakland County seat, and the county's deed office and treasurer handle the recording side of every sale in the city.

The right path depends on the house. A sound property with a clean permit history suits a listing. A property with deferred repairs, an occupant, tax trouble or an inherited title tends to move faster with a buyer who accepts it as it stands. Whichever you choose, get the offer terms on paper and have a title company confirm who owns the property and what liens are recorded.

sections.h2: What should a seller know about Pontiac's layout and history?
sections.html:
Pontiac covers 20.29 square miles, of which 19.97 are land. It is bounded by Auburn Hills on the east and north, Lake Angelus to the north, Waterford Township to the west and Bloomfield Township to the south. The Clinton River runs through downtown, where it was placed in concrete in 1963 to prevent flooding (Wikipedia, Pontiac).

Settlers arrived in 1818 and the settlement became the Oakland County seat two years later. Pontiac became a village in 1837 and a city in 1861. Carriage makers turned into auto-body builders, and General Motors assembly plants drew tens of thousands of workers in the 1910s and 1920s. The older housing near downtown, including the Fairgrove Avenue Historic District, dates from that period.

The Pontiac Silverdome opened in 1975 and hosted Detroit Lions football for years. The city has lost population since 1980 as auto jobs shrank, and the state ran its finances through an emergency manager from 2009 through 2013. The Census figures in the next section show how values stand now.

sections.h2: What do the Census figures show for Pontiac housing?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 numbers give a Pontiac median owner-occupied value of $121,700 and median gross rent of $1,063. Only 46.6% of housing is owner-occupied, the lowest rate among the four cities in this set, so many Pontiac houses are rentals.

  • Resident estimate for July 1, 2025: 62,077, up 0.8% from the April 2020 base.
  • Households: 25,617, at 2.36 persons each.
  • Median household income: $44,329.
  • Persons in poverty: 24.4%.
  • Median monthly owner costs with a mortgage: $1,223.
  • Residents living in the same house a year earlier: 87.0%.
  • Adults 25 and older with a bachelor's degree or higher: 16.1%.
  • Mean commute: 21.2 minutes.

With a large renter base and a lower median value, a seller's buyer pool in Pontiac includes small investors as well as owner-occupants. A buyer with cash can skip lender-driven repair demands, which matters on older houses.

sections.h2: How do Pontiac winters affect a house for sale?
sections.html:
Pontiac has a warm-summer continental climate and averages 36.0 inches of snow a year. The 1991 to 2020 NOAA normals show about 29 days a year with measurable snow, and 33.88 inches of total precipitation.

Record lows reach minus 22 F. Months below freezing put stress on pipes in an empty house, on the roof and on the furnace, so a vacant property should keep its heat on through the winter and have the roof and gutters looked at before showings.

sections.h2: Which roads, schools and transit connect Pontiac?
sections.html:
Woodward Avenue (M-1) runs through town and loops around downtown, Huron Street is M-59, and Telegraph Road is US 24. I-75 and its business loop pass through, and Detroit is south. Amtrak's Wolverine runs from Pontiac to Chicago via Detroit, with three trips a day each way. SMART buses serve the area, and Oakland County International Airport is in neighboring Waterford Township.

The School District of the City of Pontiac runs Pontiac High School, and four charter schools operate in the city: Pontiac Academy for Excellence, Arts and Technology Academy, Walton Charter and Great Lakes Academy. Notre Dame Preparatory is a private Catholic high school in the northeast part of the city. Buyers will ask which of these serves the address, so confirm it with the district before you list. Pontiac also has Oakland County's Water Resources Commission administering soil erosion control inside the city, which matters if you are selling a vacant lot or a house with grading work underway.

sections.h2: Do zoning and historic-district rules touch a Pontiac sale?
sections.html:
They can. The city's planning forms include Zoning Board of Appeals applications, a Historic District Approval application and a Zoning Compliance application. A house in the Fairgrove Avenue district or another historic area may need approval for exterior changes, so a buyer planning work will ask what is allowed.

Curb cuts and driveways on state trunk roads such as Woodward and Telegraph need a permit from the State of Michigan, not the city. If your lot touches one of those roads and you changed the driveway, keep the paperwork. A seller who lacks it should ask the Pontiac planning staff what applies to the parcel.

sections.h2: Does Pontiac regulate rental houses that are being sold?
sections.html:
Yes. Pontiac's code requires owners of one- and two-family dwellings that are occupied by someone other than the owner to register them with the Department of Building Safety. A new owner must re-register within 60 days after a change of ownership, and late registration draws a $25.00 fee per rental unit per month.

  • Inspections of registered dwellings may not be more than three years apart.
  • An inspection is also required before a vacated unit is reoccupied, and the owner must notify Building Safety first.
  • Occupying a unit before a certificate of compliance is issued is a municipal civil infraction with a $500.00 fine, and each day counts as a separate offense.
  • A property with a land contract recorded at the Oakland County Register of Deeds naming the occupant is exempt from the registry.

If you own a tenant-occupied Pontiac house, ask Building Safety for the certificate of compliance status before you sell. A buyer who plans to rent it will need to register within 60 days.

sections.h2: What happens at the Oakland County Register of Deeds for a Pontiac sale?
sections.html:
Recording is handled by the county, not the city. The Register of Deeds examines every document and records those that meet statutory requirements. Hand-carried documents are returned in about two weeks, and a document sent through a title company comes back about two weeks after recording.

Transfer tax applies when the consideration exceeds $99.99, and warranty deeds need a treasurer's tax certificate. The same office collects redemption payments on Sheriff Deed and Clerk Deed foreclosures, and only people with an interest in the property may redeem, so an owner facing a foreclosure sale should ask about the payoff amount before choosing a buyer.

Copies of recorded documents are available through the county, and its public index covers recorded documents back to January 1, 1964. If you inherited the house, pull the recorded chain of title early so a buyer does not hold up closing over a missing document.

The city also lists a Request for Income Tax Compliance Clearance among its income tax forms. Ask the Pontiac income tax office whether that clearance applies to your sale.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Pontiac house that has tenants in it?
faqs.a: Yes, but registration and inspection rules apply to the house. Pontiac requires one- and two-family rentals to be registered with Building Safety and inspected at least every three years, and a buyer must re-register within 60 days of the ownership change.

faqs.q: What is the fine for occupying a Pontiac rental before it passes inspection?
faqs.a: The ordinance sets a $500.00 municipal civil infraction fine, and each day is a separate offense. The owner or agent must notify Building Safety before a vacated unit is reoccupied.

faqs.q: Who records a deed in Pontiac?
faqs.a: The Oakland County Register of Deeds records it. The county examines each document, and a warranty deed needs a treasurer's tax certificate at a $5.00 fee first.

faqs.q: Does Pontiac get a lot of snow, and does it matter for a sale?
faqs.a: Pontiac averages 36.0 inches of snow a year. Roof condition, gutters and a working furnace matter most, and a vacant house needs steady heat so pipes do not freeze before the buyer's inspection.

faqs.q: What is the typical home value in Pontiac?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau reports a median owner-occupied value of $121,700 for 2020 to 2024. That is a citywide figure, so compare recent sales on your own block before accepting an offer.
